essays.stem: Explain why a housekeeping store must be kept secure, and describe the main ways of doing it.
essays.modelAnswer: The housekeeping store holds stock worth a lot of money, such as linen, amenities, chemicals and small appliances. If it is not secure, items can be stolen or misused, chemicals could reach the wrong people, and the property loses money and may run short for guests. The main ways to keep it secure are: lock the store whenever no one is working in it; allow in only authorised staff; control the keys with a signed key log; sign in and escort visitors and contractors; issue stock only against signed requisitions and record every issue; keep high-value items in a locked cage or cabinet; and carry out regular counts and spot checks. CCTV at the entrance, good lighting and secure doors and windows help too. Staff should report anything suspicious, such as a damaged lock or a stranger near the door, to the supervisor or security at once.
markingPoints: Explains the value of the stock and the risks of theft and misuse
Locked when unattended, with only authorised staff allowed in
Key control and escorted, signed-in visitors
Issues only on signed requisitions; counts and spot checks
High-value cage, CCTV or secure doors, and reporting of concerns

essays.stem: Describe how you would control keys and access to the housekeeping store, including visitors and contractors.
essays.modelAnswer: Only staff named by the supervisor may hold the store key or enter the store. When I take the key, I sign the key log with the date and time, and I sign it back in when I return it. I keep the key on me, never lend it, never leave it in the door and never take it home. If I hand it to the next shift, I do it in person and we both sign the log. If the key is lost, I report it at once so the lock can be changed. Visitors and contractors, such as a maintenance worker or a pest control officer, are signed in with their name, company, time in and reason, and I stay with them while they are in the store. When they leave, I check the area, sign them out and lock the door. I do not let anyone in just because they wear a uniform; I check with my supervisor first.
markingPoints: Only named, authorised staff hold keys or enter
Key log signed out and in; key kept on the person
Handover in person with signatures; lost key reported at once
Visitors and contractors signed in and out, with reason
Visitors escorted at all times; identity checked with the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain how stock in the store is protected from theft through issuing procedures, records and checks.
essays.modelAnswer: Stock leaves the store only when a signed requisition from an authorised person is presented. The storekeeper checks the request, issues exactly the amount approved, and both people sign. Every issue and every delivery is recorded on the stock card or in the computer, so the records always show what should be on the shelf. Regular stocktakes count everything and compare it with the records, and the supervisor also does spot checks without warning on a few items, especially high-value ones. Any difference is recounted, the paperwork is checked, and anything unexplained is reported in writing. Records are kept by the storekeeper and not left where someone could change them. Supervisors also compare the amount used with the number of rooms cleaned. Because staff know that issues are recorded and checked, theft is less likely, and if it does happen it is found quickly.
markingPoints: Issues only against signed, authorised requisitions; both sign
All issues and receipts recorded on stock cards or computer
Regular stocktakes and surprise spot checks
Differences recounted, checked and reported
Records kept secure; usage compared with rooms cleaned

essays.stem: Describe the cleaning schedule and the method you would follow to keep a housekeeping store clean.
essays.modelAnswer: The store has a written cleaning schedule. Daily, I sweep or vacuum and damp-mop the floor, empty the bins, remove empty boxes and wipe up any spills. Weekly, I dust and wipe every shelf, check for pests and damp, and check that labels are in place. Monthly, or as the schedule says, there is a deep clean: moving stock, washing shelves and walls, cleaning light fittings and checking behind and under the shelving. For the method, I put on gloves and closed shoes, put out a wet-floor sign, and read the label of each chemical. I work from top to bottom and from the back to the door, so dust falls onto areas not yet cleaned. I move stock aside, clean, let the shelf dry, then return the stock in the right order, oldest at the front. I sign and date the cleaning checklist and report any problem I find.
markingPoints: Daily tasks: floor, bins, boxes, spills
Weekly and deep-clean tasks
PPE, wet-floor sign and correct chemicals
Top to bottom, back to front; stock moved and returned in order
Checklist signed and dated; problems reported

essays.stem: Explain how to prevent pests in a store, and what to do if you find signs of them.
essays.modelAnswer: To prevent pests, the store is kept clean and dry, with no food or drink allowed inside. Doors are kept closed, gaps around pipes and doors are sealed, and damaged screens are reported. Stock is kept on shelves off the floor and away from the walls so the floor can be cleaned and checked. Empty cardboard is removed quickly, because pests hide and breed in it. Stock is rotated so nothing sits for months. The property's pest control contractor visits regularly. If I find signs of pests, such as droppings, gnawed packaging, nests, live insects or a bad smell, I do not try to use home sprays. I report it at once to my supervisor, record it in the pest log, and take damaged or soiled stock out of use. The contractor treats the problem, and the area is cleaned and checked again afterwards.
markingPoints: Clean, dry store with no food or drink
Doors closed and gaps sealed
Shelves off the floor and away from walls; cardboard removed; stock rotated
Signs of pests named (droppings, gnawing, live insects)
Report and log it, remove damaged stock, contractor treats it

essays.stem: Explain how chemicals, linen and guest amenities should be arranged in a store so they stay clean, safe and in good condition.
essays.modelAnswer: Each type of stock has its own labelled area. Chemicals are kept in their original or properly labelled containers, closed tightly, on low shelves, apart from linen and amenities, in a ventilated area, with the safety data sheets and a spill kit nearby. Products that react together, such as bleach and acid or ammonia cleaners, are kept apart in case they leak. Linen is kept on clean, dry, slatted shelves, away from walls, chemicals and soiled linen, so it does not get damp, stained or smelly. Guest amenities and paper goods are kept clean and dry, off the floor, in their boxes, with the oldest at the front. Heavy items go on low shelves, light items higher up, and nothing is stacked to the ceiling. The store is kept cool, dry and well lit, so stock does not spoil and labels can be read.
markingPoints: Separate, labelled areas for each type of stock
Chemicals: labelled, closed, low, ventilated, SDS and spill kit
Reacting chemicals kept apart
Linen and amenities kept clean, dry, off the floor and away from chemicals
Heavy items low, oldest at the front; cool, dry, lit store

essays.stem: Describe the main fire and personal safety points to follow in a housekeeping store.
essays.modelAnswer: For fire safety, no smoking or naked flames are allowed in or near the store. Exits and aisles are kept clear, and the fire extinguisher is kept by the door, checked and not blocked. Stock is not stacked up to the ceiling or around sprinkler heads, as the fire rules say. Empty cardboard and waste are removed quickly, and paper or linen is never stored next to lights, heaters or electrical panels. Faulty lights or sockets are reported. For personal safety, I wear closed shoes and gloves, and eye protection with chemicals. I lift with bent knees and a straight back, use a trolley for heavy loads, and use a checked step stool for high shelves, never a box or a shelf. Spills are cleaned at once with a wet-floor sign out. I never mix chemicals, and I know where the first-aid kit is.
markingPoints: No smoking or flames; extinguisher ready and not blocked
Exits and aisles clear; no stacking to ceiling or sprinklers
Waste and cardboard removed; nothing near lights or heaters; faults reported
PPE and safe lifting, with a trolley or step stool
Spills cleaned with a sign out; chemicals never mixed

essays.stem: Describe what you would do if you suspected theft from the store, or found signs of a break-in.
essays.modelAnswer: If I suspect theft, for example because a count is short or I see a co-worker taking items, I do not accuse anyone or try to deal with it myself. I recount and check the paperwork, then report the facts calmly and privately to my supervisor or security, with dates, items and amounts, and I write them down. If I find signs of a break-in, such as a forced lock, a broken window or stock thrown about, I do not go in alone if someone may still be inside. I keep away, call security or the supervisor, and keep other people away. I do not touch or tidy anything, because security or the police may need to see it as it is. Later I help to check what is missing against the records and write a statement. Until the lock or window is repaired, the store must be watched or kept secure another way.
markingPoints: Does not accuse or act alone
Recounts and checks paperwork, then reports facts privately
Break-in: does not enter alone; calls security; keeps others away
Does not touch or tidy, so evidence is kept
Helps check losses, writes a statement; store kept secure until repaired

essays.stem: Explain how damp, heat and poor ventilation affect stored items, and what you can do about them.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica's climate is hot and humid, so stores need care. Damp air and poor ventilation let mould and mildew grow on linen, paper and cardboard, giving black spots and a musty smell; linen may have to be rewashed or thrown out. Damp also softens boxes, so stacks can collapse, and it attracts pests. Heat can make some chemicals and aerosols unsafe, can spoil amenities such as lotions and soaps, and can make stock age faster. To prevent this, the store should have good airflow from vents, fans or air conditioning, as the property provides. Stock is kept off the floor and away from walls, and never put away damp. Leaks and wet patches are reported at once. Doors are kept closed in heavy rain. Items that are sensitive to heat are stored away from windows, roofs and hot pipes, and the store is checked regularly for smells and spots.
markingPoints: Damp and poor air flow cause mould and smells on linen and paper
Damp weakens boxes and attracts pests
Heat spoils amenities and makes some chemicals unsafe
Good ventilation; stock off the floor and away from walls; never stored damp
Leaks reported; heat-sensitive items kept away from heat; regular checks

essays.stem: Describe how you would close and secure the housekeeping store at the end of the day.
essays.modelAnswer: Before closing, I finish any issues and make sure all requisitions are signed and recorded. I put away any stock left out, close all containers, and check that no chemicals are leaking. I clean up spills, empty the bins, take out cardboard and sweep the floor, then sign the daily cleaning checklist. I check that no one is left inside and that the high-value cage or cabinet is locked. I switch off lights and any equipment that should be off, and check that windows are shut and locked. I lock the door and test that it is secure. Then I return the key and sign the key log, or hand the key over in person to the person on duty. Finally I report anything unusual, such as a broken lock, a leak or a stock difference, to the supervisor or write it in the logbook.
markingPoints: Finishes and records issues; puts away stock
Cleans up, empties bins and signs the cleaning checklist
Checks no one is inside and the high-value cage is locked
Lights off, windows shut, door locked and tested
Key returned and signed in; problems reported or logged

practical1.title: Deep clean and reorganise a housekeeping store
practical1.brief: As a group, deep clean and reorganise the Centre's housekeeping store (or a store area the assessor sets up with linen, amenities, paper goods, cleaning chemicals and some equipment). First walk through the store, note any hazards, pests, damp or damaged stock on a checklist, and agree who does what. Each member is responsible for one bay or section: they move the stock aside, dust and wipe the shelves from top to bottom, clean and disinfect as the cleaning schedule says, and put the stock back in order, with heavy items low, chemicals low and apart from linen and amenities, oldest stock at the front and every shelf labelled. One member (or all, in turn) cleans the floor from the back towards the door with a wet-floor sign out. Remove cardboard and waste, set aside damaged or expired items, and complete and sign the store cleaning checklist. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and checklist to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The Centre's store (or a set-up store) with mixed stock
Cleaning cloths, buckets, mop, broom and dustpan
Neutral cleaner and disinfectant, with labels and safety data sheets
Gloves, closed shoes and eye protection
Store cleaning checklist and a walk-through hazard checklist
photos: The store before cleaning, from the door
Each member's bay emptied and cleaned
Each bay restocked, labelled, with heavy items and chemicals low
The floor being cleaned with the wet-floor sign out
Damaged or expired items set aside and labelled
The finished store and the signed cleaning checklist
checklist: Wore the right PPE and read the chemical labels
Cleaned their bay top to bottom with the right products
Put stock back in order, oldest at the front
Kept chemicals low and apart from linen and amenities
Stacked safely, with nothing blocking exits or the extinguisher
Removed cardboard and waste; set aside damaged stock
Signed the checklist and reported any problem found
safety: Never mix chemicals; use them as the label says
Use a step stool, never a shelf or box, to reach high shelves
Lift with bent knees or use the trolley; share heavy loads
Put out a wet-floor sign and keep exits and the extinguisher clear

practical2.title: Store security check, spot count and closing procedure
practical2.brief: Your group carries out a security check of the Centre's housekeeping store (or a set-up store). Each member leads one part while the others assist: (1) a security walk-round using the assessor's checklist (locks, windows, lighting, cage, CCTV or alarm if fitted, exits, signs of entry); (2) a spot count of 10 items chosen by the assessor, compared with the stock records, with any difference recounted and written up; (3) a role play of issuing stock against a requisition, including refusing an unsigned request politely; (4) a role play of signing in and escorting a contractor, using the visitor log and the key log; (5) closing and securing the store and handing over the key (in a group of four, parts 4 and 5 are shared). Finish with a short written report to the supervisor listing what you found and at least three recommendations. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, forms and report to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Stock records for the items to be counted
photos: The spot count sheet compared with the records
The requisition role play, with the signed form
The contractor sign-in and the key log entries
The store locked at closing, with the key log signed
The written report to the supervisor
checklist: Checked locks, windows, lighting and exits carefully
Counted accurately and recounted any difference
Issued stock only against a signed requisition
Refused an unsigned request politely and correctly
Signed in and escorted the contractor; used the key log correctly
Closed and secured the store and handed over the key correctly
Wrote clear findings and sensible recommendations
safety: Do not enter the store alone if there are signs of a break-in; tell the assessor
Never test an alarm or CCTV without permission
Use a step stool to reach high stock during the count
Keep the findings confidential to the group and the assessor
